blocks.text: An 82-year-old woman slips on a rug. She cannot get up, and her right leg lies shortened and turned outwards. The X-ray shows a displaced fracture of the neck of the femur. The surgeon's main worry is not the break itself but whether the femoral head, cut off from its blood supply, will survive.

blocks.markdown: The **hip joint** carries body weight from the pelvis to the lower limb and must be both strong and mobile. The **thigh** between hip and knee is divided by fascial septa into three muscle compartments, each with a typical nerve supply and function. Understanding the bony landmarks, the blood supply of the femoral head and the compartment pattern gives you the anatomy behind hip fracture, thigh weakness and sciatic injury.

blocks.title: Hip joint
blocks.text: A synovial ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone (formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis). The acetabulum is deepened by a fibrocartilaginous labrum; the joint is surrounded by a strong capsule reinforced by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments. The hip is much more stable than the shoulder but has less range of movement.

rows: Iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), anterior inferior iliac spine
ASIS is a surface landmark; sartorius arises from the ASIS and rectus femoris from the anterior inferior iliac spine
Hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity; sit-bone when seated
Lunate (articular) surface, acetabular fossa, acetabular notch, transverse acetabular ligament
Socket for the femoral head; the ligament of the head of the femur attaches to the fossa
Head with fovea capitis, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line (front) and crest (back), linea aspera, gluteal tuberosity
Greater trochanter receives gluteus medius and minimus; lesser trochanter receives iliopsoas; the neck is the site of hip fracture
blocks.caption: Bony landmarks of the pelvis and proximal femur.

blocks.markdown: The **neck of the femur** joins the head to the shaft at an angle (the neck-shaft or angle of inclination, about 125 degrees in adults, with some variation). It lies mostly inside the joint capsule: the capsule attaches in front along the intertrochanteric line, but behind it attaches partway along the neck, so the posterior part of the neck lies outside. Fractures of the neck are therefore called **intracapsular**, and fractures at or below the trochanters are **extracapsular**.

blocks.title: Blood supply of the femoral head
blocks.text: The main supply comes from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (branches of the profunda femoris artery), which form an arterial ring around the base of the neck. From this ring, retinacular arteries run up along the neck beneath the capsule to the head; the medial circumflex femoral artery is the most important contributor. A small additional supply, the artery of the ligament of the head of the femur (from the obturator artery), is usually insufficient in adults. A displaced intracapsular fracture tears the retinacular arteries and can leave the head ischaemic, causing avascular necrosis.

blocks.title: Fracture level and risk to the head
blocks.prompt: Compare the likely blood supply of the femoral head after (a) a displaced intracapsular fracture of the neck and (b) an extracapsular intertrochanteric fracture.

steps.text: Retinacular arteries run along the neck inside the capsule, so a displaced intracapsular fracture tears them.
The artery of the ligament of the head provides little supply in adults, so the head can be ischaemic.
An intertrochanteric fracture lies below the capsule attachment, so the retinacular arteries and arterial ring remain intact.

blocks.answer: A displaced intracapsular neck fracture risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head; an extracapsular fracture usually does not, because the retinacular supply is preserved.

blocks.markdown: **The thigh compartments.** Three fascial compartments are separated by intermuscular septa that pass from the fascia lata to the femur. Each has its own nerve supply.

rows: Sartorius; quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius); iliacus and psoas major at the top; pectineus
Femoral nerve (L2-L4); psoas by direct branches of lumbar rami; pectineus by femoral nerve
Adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, gracilis, obturator externus
Obturator nerve (L2-L4); the hamstring part of adductor magnus by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve
Biceps femoris (long and short heads), semitendinosus, semimembranosus
Sciatic nerve (tibial part; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular part)
blocks.caption: Compartments of the thigh. Pectineus is usually described as being supplied by the femoral nerve (sometimes with an obturator contribution).

blocks.title: Predicting weakness from a nerve injury
blocks.prompt: A patient cannot extend the knee against gravity and has numbness over the front of the thigh. Which compartment and nerve are involved?

steps.text: Knee extension is produced by quadriceps femoris, which is in the anterior compartment.
The anterior compartment is supplied by the femoral nerve.
The femoral nerve also gives anterior cutaneous branches to the front of the thigh, consistent with the numbness.

blocks.answer: The anterior compartment, supplied by the femoral nerve.

items: Anterior: femoral nerve; extends the knee, flexes the hip.
Medial: obturator nerve; adducts the thigh.
Posterior: sciatic nerve (tibial part, plus common fibular for the short head of biceps femoris); extends the hip, flexes the knee.

blocks.title: Intracapsular versus extracapsular
blocks.text: Do not describe all hip fractures as 'neck of femur' fractures. Only fractures within the capsule are intracapsular and threaten the head's blood supply; intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric fractures are extracapsular and are managed differently.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical picture.** In a displaced fracture of the neck of the femur, the pull of the muscles shortens the limb and the leg is typically laterally rotated. A shortened, externally rotated leg in an older patient after a fall should prompt consideration of this fracture.

points: The hip is a stable ball-and-socket joint formed by the femoral head and the acetabulum; the proximal femur has a head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line and crest.
The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery; displaced intracapsular neck fractures risk avascular necrosis.
Thigh compartments: anterior (femoral nerve), medial (obturator nerve) and posterior (sciatic nerve).

questions.stem: Which bony landmark of the femur receives the tendon of iliopsoas?

distractorRationale.b: The greater trochanter receives gluteus medius and minimus.
distractorRationale.c: The gluteal tuberosity receives gluteus maximus.
distractorRationale.d: The fovea capitis receives the ligament of the head of the femur.

questions.explanation: Iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur and is the principal hip flexor. Remembering which muscles attach to which landmark helps predict the effect of avulsion injuries.

questions.stem: Which artery provides the main blood supply to the head of the femur in adults?

options.text: Medial circumflex femoral artery (via retinacular branches)
Artery of the ligament of the head of the femur

questions.correctOptionText: Medial circumflex femoral artery (via retinacular branches)

distractorRationale.b: This artery is a small supply, usually insufficient in adults.
distractorRationale.c: The superior gluteal artery supplies gluteal muscles.
distractorRationale.d: The popliteal artery is behind the knee.

questions.explanation: The medial circumflex femoral artery, a branch of the profunda femoris, gives retinacular arteries that run up the neck to supply the head. The artery of the ligament of the head is a minor additional source.

questions.stem: Why does a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck risk avascular necrosis of the head?

options.text: It tears the retinacular arteries running along the neck inside the capsule
It disrupts the obturator externus tendon

questions.correctOptionText: It tears the retinacular arteries running along the neck inside the capsule

distractorRationale.b: Nerve injury does not cause avascular necrosis.
distractorRationale.c: The popliteal artery lies behind the knee, away from the hip.
distractorRationale.d: Obturator externus does not supply the head.

questions.explanation: The retinacular arteries run along the surface of the neck beneath the capsule, so a displaced intracapsular fracture tears them. Because the ligament of the head supplies little blood in adults, the head may become ischaemic.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris?

distractorRationale.b: The obturator nerve supplies the adductors.
distractorRationale.c: The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings.
distractorRationale.d: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus.

questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris and sartorius belong to the anterior compartment and are supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4). Damage to this nerve abolishes knee extension.

questions.stem: Which muscle group belongs to the medial compartment of the thigh and is supplied mainly by the obturator nerve?

options.text: Adductor longus, adductor brevis and gracilis
Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae

questions.correctOptionText: Adductor longus, adductor brevis and gracilis

distractorRationale.b: These are in the anterior compartment (femoral nerve).
distractorRationale.c: These are hamstrings in the posterior compartment (sciatic nerve).
distractorRationale.d: These are gluteal muscles supplied by gluteal nerves.

questions.explanation: The medial compartment contains the adductors and gracilis, supplied by the obturator nerve. Adductor magnus has a dual supply, with its hamstring part supplied by the sciatic nerve.

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the hamstring muscles semitendinosus and semimembranosus?

options.text: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve

distractorRationale.b: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior compartment.
distractorRationale.c: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment.
distractorRationale.d: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.

questions.explanation: The posterior compartment is supplied by the sciatic nerve, specifically its tibial part for semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of biceps femoris. The short head of biceps is supplied by the common fibular part.

questions.stem: True or false: the short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.

distractorRationale.a: The short head is supplied by the common fibular part.

questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris is the only hamstring muscle supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve. The long head is supplied by the tibial division.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman falls and presents with a shortened, externally rotated right leg. Radiograph shows a displaced fracture through the neck of the femur within the capsule. Which complication is she most at risk of?

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Foot drop from femoral nerve injury
Compartment syndrome of the anterior leg

questions.correctOptionText: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

distractorRationale.b: Foot drop is related to the common fibular nerve, not the femoral nerve.
distractorRationale.c: Wrist drop is a radial nerve problem.
distractorRationale.d: Compartment syndrome is not the characteristic complication of intracapsular neck fractures.

questions.explanation: The displaced intracapsular fracture tears the retinacular arteries that supply the head. The head can therefore become avascular, which is why such fractures are often treated with replacement rather than fixation.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a thigh compartment with its nerve supply?

distractorRationale.b: The anterior compartment is supplied by the femoral nerve.
distractorRationale.c: The posterior compartment is supplied by the sciatic nerve.
distractorRationale.d: The medial compartment is supplied by the obturator nerve.

questions.explanation: Anterior is femoral, medial is obturator and posterior is sciatic. Exceptions such as pectineus and the hamstring part of adductor magnus are best learned as exceptions to this pattern.

questions.stem: Describe the blood supply of the head of the femur and explain its clinical significance after fracture of the neck of the femur.
markingGuide: Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (from the profunda femoris) form an arterial ring around the neck.
Retinacular arteries ascend along the neck beneath the capsule to the head; the medial circumflex is the most important.
A small contribution comes from the artery of the ligament of the head (from the obturator artery).
In a displaced intracapsular fracture the retinacular arteries are torn.
Result: avascular necrosis of the head, so replacement is often considered rather than fixation.
questions.explanation: The blood supply runs along the neck within the capsule, which makes it vulnerable. This anatomical fact guides surgical choice and explains the risk of avascular necrosis.

questions.stem: List the muscles of the anterior, medial and posterior compartments of the thigh and give the nerve supply of each compartment.
markingGuide: Anterior: sartorius, quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris and three vasti), pectineus; femoral nerve.
Medial: adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis, obturator externus; obturator nerve.
Posterior: biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus; sciatic nerve (tibial part).
Mention exceptions: hamstring part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve; short head of biceps by the common fibular part.
questions.explanation: Remembering each compartment's nerve gives a framework for muscle supply. The exceptions occur because some muscles combine tissue from different embryological groups.
